title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami
content_c:
Flávio Bolsonaro declared himself the “true president” of Brazil after losing last Sunday’s presidential election and fleeing to the United States.
After landing on a private jet with his family in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday morning, the far-right senator published the claim in a letter – even though his own party has recognised the legitimate victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as have all of Brazil’s institutions, and international observers who monitored and endorsed the vote.
Brazil’s three main newspapers – Folha de S.Paulo, O Globo and O Estado de S.Paulo – all described Bolsonaro’s declaration as “coup-mongering”.
The senator later deleted the letter and published a new one in which, instead of calling himself the “true president”, he described himself as “the leader of Brazil”.
After losing Sunday’s runoff vote to Lula, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.
From there he boarded a Gulfstream IV, registered LV-JQW, which had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.
Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, took off on the jet with his wife and two teenage daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador and continued on to the Miami-Opa Locka airport, a private aviation hub about 11 miles north of downtown Miami catering to corporate executives and wealthy travelers.
Bolsonaro, wearing a black bulletproof vest and looking somber, and his family emerged from the plane into a postcard-perfect sunny south Florida morning at 9.24am. They briefly remained inside the airport before leaving, shielded by black umbrellas, climbing into a dark gray Ford Expedition Max and speeding away under police escort.
Bolsonaro said nothing to reporters before boarding the vehicle and the mood was low-key, without any supporters present to welcome him and only two dozen journalists who were kept at a distance by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.
In the letter, published about seven hours after his arrival, Bolsonaro also thanked Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, “for his courage, sense of justice and legality”, and Donald Trump “and the wonderful American people for welcoming me”.
He again repeated, without evidence, his claim that there had been “electoral fraud” – a claim rejected by Brazil’s electoral court and supreme court, as well as the presidents of the lower house and senate. Bolsonaro’s party said on Monday: “We recognise the presidential result.”
At least three different versions of the letter were published by Bolsonaro and his allies, including one that used the country’s pre-1968 name and the English spelling “Brazil” rather than the Portuguese “Brasil” – which some saw as another sign of the Bolsonaro clan’s subservience to the US.
Brazilian newspapers reported that Bolsonaro and his family had been granted humanitarian visas in the US. On Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.
“They’re fine people. … I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flávio a little bit. I know the father very well,” the US president said.
On Wednesday, however, when asked about Bolsonaro’s claim, Trump said he would stay out of Brazil’s post-election turmoil.
“Well, I’m not going to make a comment about that, but I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see,” he said. “But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”
Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.
Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him from leaving the country.
There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies, at about 6pm on Monday, and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.
The Argentinian newspaper Página/12 reported that the aircraft belonged to the businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated by local police in one of the biggest scandals of Javier Milei’s administration, involving the alleged payment of bribes linked to the purchase of medicines for people with disabilities.
Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one of them examining suspicions that the senator was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
It was in connection with that case that, shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.
Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.
O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.
Fleeing Brazil has almost become standard practice among Bolsonaro supporters facing criminal charges or convictions in the country: about a dozen politicians or influencers closely aligned with Jair Bolsonaro have done the same in recent years.
The former president himself spent three months in Florida shortly after losing the 2022 election. He later returned to Brazil and, while facing trial over the attempted coup, spent two nights at the Hungarian embassy in Brasília, then run by his ally Viktor Orbán.
While under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison, the patriarch of the Bolsonaro clan used a soldering iron in an attempt to destroy his electronic ankle monitor.

title: Budget 2026: £100 energy payment for millions and rise in bank tax as watchdog warns on stalling living standards – as it happened
content_c:
OBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decade
The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.
Our central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.
Here are comments on the budget from a Guardian panel, comprising Polly Toynbee, Hettie O’Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik, and John McDonnell.
And here is Polly’s conclusion.
Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.
Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist and a Treasury minister under David Cameron, told the PM programme that he thought it was sensible for John Healey not to “rock the boat” with this budget. He said his old City friends were pleasantly surprised by what was in it.
My friends in my old world of business and investing, from the ones that have contacted me, every single one of them has been slightly positively surprised by what was announced today.
Treasury minister Torsten Bell rejects charge budget lacks 'ending 40 years of neoliberalism' ambition
Torsten Bell, the Treasury minister, has just finished an interview on Radio 4’s PM programme. Asked about claims (like this one, assuming the MP is being sarcastic, or ours at 8.50am) that the budget did not live up to Andy Burnham’s ambitions to end 40 years of neoliberalism, Bell said he did not accept that. In many areas, the government was taking a very different approach, he argued. He said Margaret Thatcher hollowed out local government, while today’s fiscal devolution roadmap will reverse that. He also said the proposals to change the way energy pricing works (see 12.50pm) would transformative.
Here is a chart from the fiscal devolution roadmap document setting out what rules will change, and when.
MSAs are mayoral strategic authorities, and FSA are foundation strategic authorities, equivalent bodies which do not have a mayor to lead them.
Minister dismisses as 'garbage' Tory and Lib Dem claims that defence spending actually being cut
A Treasury minister has dismissed as “garbage” opposition claims that the small print in the budget book shows that John Healey is actually cutting defence spending.
The budget red book says that, while £42.6bn had been set aside for MoD spending in 2027-28, that has now been revised down to £41.1bn.
The Treasury says this is because less money than expected is needed for pensions. But James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, said that not allocating the unused money for other areas of defence spending was “a complete dereliction of duty from the chancellor”.
And James MacClearly, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, made the same argument. He said:
It is disgraceful that after pitching Labour as serious on defence, Healey and [Wes] Streeting are cutting the military’s resource budget by nearly £1bn next year. This will leave our troops worse off and undermine our security.
In response, Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister, posted this on social media.
Absolute garbage - this is a technical change that happens when public sector pension contributions change. There’s no impact on defence spending power & the Tories used the same mechanism in govt. What does matter for defence spending? The chancellor, who has increased it
Today’s ‘picky bits’ budget has pushed tough decisions into next year, says Tim Sarson, head of tax policy at KPMG UK:
“When it comes to tax rises, as expected with his options limited by the 2024 manifesto, the chancellor was left with a pick and mix or ‘picky bits’ approach.
Overall the announcements today will raise £7bn per year by 2031-32 with some winners and losers including a widely trailed bank surcharge, which came in lower than expected at 3% and further taxes on the gambling sector
James Smith, ING’s developed markets economist in the UK, says the budget has left more questions than answers.
Those questions include:
How will the government account for higher inflation in departmental budgets? How will it fund defence? Both questions were left unanswered today. The government’s overall spending pot for government departments was left largely unchanged later this decade, despite a higher path for inflation and the chancellor’s reaffirmed commitment to 3% Nato spending by 2030. Implicitly, that pledge is being funded by squeezing other areas of government; the OBR’s numbers imply real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year for unprotected departments later this decade.
That almost certainly won’t happen – and this is before you take social care or any of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s other bold policies into account.
These thorny issues have been punted into 2027, potentially in the autumn, when the government will have to unveil its long-awaited spending review.
The NewEconomicsFoundation says the budget is a missed opportunity to bring down inflation, through more ambitious cost of living measures.
They say:
The chancellor has missed an opportunity to bring down inflation rates, according to analysis from the New Economics Foundation (NEF). The research suggests a more ambitious package of cost-of-living policies would take inflation from the OBR’s projected 3.64% to 2.88% by June 2027.
But CapitalEconomics say the chancellor has done enough to keep the markets on side.
Today’s UK budget announcement has proven the non-event that newly-minted Chancellor Healey had signalled in advance. While his first budget is hardly inspiring, it contrasts favourably with the initial efforts of some of his recent predecessors.
By sticking to a gradual fiscal tightening path, and to the expectations set over the past couple of months for a muddle-through budget, Healey has probably done enough to keep the Gilt market on side for now.
We think that Gilt yields will fall over the coming year as the UK’s fiscal risk premium remains contained and the Bank of England policy takes a less hawkish path than money markets discount.
Ministerial direction needed for £6.5bn loan for Ukraine after export finance agency warns of 'exceptionally high' risk of default
The government needed to issue a ministerial direction to get UK Export Finance to approve a £3bn increase in lending for Ukraine, it emerged today. This is a procedure that happens when a civil servant judges that a decision is not justified under normal responsible public spending rules, and insists that it can only go ahead if a minister explicitly overrules the objections.
In his letter explaining the need for a ministerial direction, Tim Reid, UKEF’s chief executive, argued that this was not a core obligation for the agency (which is there to help British exporters, not to fight Russia) and that the risk of the £6.5bn not being paid back was too high.
Reid said:
UKEF has played a significant role in delivering the government’s support to Ukraine by staying on cover with £3.5bn of capacity to provide export finance, supporting strategically important transactions including the supply of nuclear fuel, reconstruction of critical infrastructure and air-defence missiles. These have supported Ukraine’s resilience at a critical time while also creating jobs and industrial capacity across the UK.
However, the financial risks associated with UKEF providing support in Ukraine remain far beyond those that we would normally be willing to accept. The probability of default and expected loss is exceptionally high …
UKEF is close to capacity against its existing £3.5bn limit. You have now asked me to consider a £3bn increase in UKEF’s cover limit, taking UKEF’s Ukraine country risk limit to £6.5bn.
In response, Jonathan Reynolds, the business secetary, said he was issuing a ministerial direction because “the United Kingdom has been steadfast in its support for Ukraine’s defence, economic resilience and long-term recovery, and I consider UKEF’s support to be an important component of that wider effort.”
OBR: Employment Rights Act will have negative impact on economy
Labour’s Employment Rights Act is likely to have a negative impact on the economy, the OBR says today.
This is the first time that the OBR has assessed the potential economic impacts of the ERA, which received royal assent at the end of last year.
And the fiscal watchdog has concluded the ERA will probably have a negative impact on potential output, though it isn’t making an explicit assessment today.
The OBR says:
Our analysis suggests that the ERA will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses, particularly through increased uncertainty, lost flexibility and higher labour related costs, which will more than offset any potential positive impact on worker productivity.
That fits with the government’s own analysis, which said the reforms could cost businesses up to £5bn a year.
How budget includes £10bn in extra support for Ukraine
Earlier John Healey got an endorsement for what he said about defence spending from Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general. (See 2.15pm.)
George Robertson, the former Nato secretary general and the lead author of the strategic defence review, has also welcomed Healey’s defence announcements. (See 1.30pm.) He said:
John Healey is acting in the national interest – and has done exactly what he said was needed for defence in his resignation letter, by setting a headmark for 3% in 2030.”
I am strongly in favour of innovative ways of financing defence – and this is a credible route to get more into UK defence. Today’s annoucements strengthens UK leadership in Nato once again.
In his speech Healey announced an extra £10bn in economic support for Ukraine. This Treasury news release explains where that money is going. It says:
The £10bn package includes £7bn of economic support being made available over three years, including up to £5.5bn of World Bank guarantees and a £500m grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility, mobilising £1.5bn of support for Ukraine.
Alongside this, there will be a £3bn increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) capacity for Ukraine, prioritised for military support. It will bring the total UKEF support to £6.5bn.
What business organisations are saying about budget
Business groups have given the budget a mixed reaction.
Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the CBI, welcomed some measures, but argued John Healey should have done more for growth. She said
On the face of it, this budget lacks the bold moves that would have made it easier for firms to invest, hire and grow.
At a time of exceptional geopolitical pressures, using some fiscal headroom to absorb genuine short-term shocks is preferable to loading additional permanent costs onto business and weakening investment.
Slowing the convergence of youth rates with the national living wage is a sensible move in face of the Neets crisis and current labour market pressures. But the chancellor could have gone further. Reducing the cost of hiring by increasing the employer NICs threshold would have given firms more space to create entry-level jobs and boost employment.
Jonathan Geldart, director general at the Institute of Directors, said his members were relieved.
Business leaders will be relieved that the chancellor’s budget included no nasty surprises, having been conditioned in previous budgets to expect the worst. We very much welcome the numerous measures intended to support British start-ups and scale-ups, such as the new Founders’ Relief, Young Entrepreneurs Allowance and EMI2 [enterprise management incentive] share incentives (as well as support for small brewers).
What might at first blush be a case of small beer today could start adding up to something promising in the future.
But Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said the budget was a disappointment.
This budget should have been the moment to help small businesses with the soaring costs holding them back, and the taxes restricting job creation. Instead, they got nothing to ease sky-high energy bills and nothing to make hiring someone more affordable, while the increase in business rates relief excludes too many.
A JP Morgan spokesperson has criticised the decision to hike the UK’s bank tax today, arguing that targeting one of the UK’s most lucrative sectors “lacks principle”:
“We are committed to the country, and we recognise the cost of living challenges there and the global economic headwinds that it faces, but to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.
“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”
But despite the bank’s disappointment, JP Morgan is due to charge ahead with its £3bn new UK HQ, according to a source familiar with the matter.
What opposition parties are saying about the budget
Kemi Badenoch’s reaction to the budget on behalf of the Conservative party was covered earlier, at 2.11pm. Here is some reaction from other oppostion parties.
The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, told MPs that John Healey should have done more to address the problems with Brexit. He said:
I do think this budget will be more defined by Labour’s red lines on Europe and the Conservatives’ Brexit red tape, rather than faster growth.
And at the root of so much of what’s gone wrong in our country – the cost of living crisis, higher taxes, broken public services, empty high streets, the lack of jobs and opportunity – at the root of all of that is the lack of economic growth.
Our economy is being held back. British business is being held back, and it’s been held back above all by the terrible damage of the Conservative Brexit deal.
Ellie Chowns, the Green party Treasury spokesperson, said the budget was lacking in ambition.
You’d have thought that, after going to the trouble of ousting the last PM, taking his job, and installing a brand-new chancellor, Andy Burnham would be keen to ensure Labour displayed a bit more ambition at today’s budget than it did under his predecessor.
Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.
There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media, he said:
These are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.
Unemployment will rise to 5% in 2027.
The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.
By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …
We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:
The UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.
This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.
Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.
Ben Lake, Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.
Today’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.
After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition
The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.
UK gambling firms' value jumps after chancellor resisted large duty hike
Rob Davies
Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.
Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts, Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), RankGroup (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year, also warned that closures and job losses would follow.
The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.
Burnham rules out general election in the next year
Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation (including among economists and investors) that he could seek to consolidate his position.
He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.
The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget.
He said:
“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.
“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.
“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”
He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.
He said:
“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”
Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.
AndrewWishart, senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.
He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.
Wishart says:
The big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.
More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”
Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management, says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.
Like last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.
“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”
BenjaminJones, Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:
“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.
His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.
John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.
The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

Lewis said:The chancellor said he will be talking to Ofgem about how they get rid of the charge on electricity as well, but that is ‘trickier’ apparently and will take longer. Continue reading...
author: Andrew Sparrow and Graeme Wearden

OBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decade
The OBR report says RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.
Our central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.
Here are comments on the budget from a Guardian panel, comprising Polly Toynbee, Hettie O’Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik, and John McDonnell.
And here is Polly’s conclusion.
Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.
Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist and a Treasury minister under David Cameron, told the PM programme that he thought it was sensible for John Healey not to “rock the boat” with this budget. He said his old City friends were pleasantly surprised by what was in it.
My friends in my old world of business and investing, from the ones that have contacted me, every single one of them has been slightly positively surprised by what was announced today.
Treasury minister Torsten Bell rejects charge budget lacks 'ending 40 years of neoliberalism' ambition
Torsten Bell, the Treasury minister, has just finished an interview on Radio 4’s PM programme. Asked about claims (like this one, assuming the MP is being sarcastic, or ours at 8.50am) that the budget did not live up to Andy Burnham’s ambitions to end 40 years of neoliberalism, Bell said he did not accept that. In many areas, the government was taking a very different approach, he argued. He said Margaret Thatcher hollowed out local government, while today’s fiscal devolution roadmap will reverse that. He also said the proposals to change the way energy pricing works (see 12.50pm) would transformative.

Unfortunately, what Britain actually saw today was a business-as-usual budget which failed to engage with the real issues facing our country – choosing to tinker round the edges, rather than properly taxing extreme wealth and profits, making essentials genuinely and permanently affordable, or investing in our long-term climate resilience.
There was no discussion of the climate crisis in Healey’s speech today, nor any new investment in renewables and climate adaptation, despite the devastating impact of this summer’s deadly heatwaves and wildfires on our communities, public services, and economy.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said Britain was broke. In a post on social media, he said:
These are the stats John Healey doesn’t want you to read.
Unemployment will rise to 5% in 2027.
The tax burden is going up AGAIN to the highest since WW2.
By 2031 we’ll be spending £160bn/year on debt interest alone – up £36bn/year …
We are on a fiscal knife-edge. Britain is Broke. Britain needs Reform.
Kirsty Blackman, the SNP’s economy spokesperson at Westminster, said this was not a budget for Scotland. She said:
The UK Budget shows the Labour government doesn’t get Scotland – and isn’t doing anywhere near enough to protect people from the looming cost of living emergency this winter.
This isn’t a budget that a Scottish chancellor would have delivered. Instead of providing meaningful help, it has abandoned families in the face of soaring bills and has imposed another betrayal on Scotland’s energy – with the decision to scrap Scottish carbon capture funding.
Andy Burnham promised to cut the cost of living but every major household bill has increased on his watch – and the UK budget completely fails to address the scale of the challenge families are now facing.
Ben Lake, Plaid Cymru’s economic spokeperson at Westminster, said Wales was just an afterthought in the budget.
Today’s budget was UK Labour’s opportunity to prove that Wales is more than an afterthought in Treasury decisions. Instead, it appears to have delivered the worst funding settlement for Wales in years.
After months of promises about a new relationship with Wales and a new approach from the Treasury, the question many people will be asking is – where is the ambition
The chancellor chose not to announce what Wales would receive in consequentials from this budget. Buried in the documents is around £450 million of additional funding spread over three years. That falls well short of keeping pace with inflation and risks forcing the kind of spending reductions Wales experienced during the worst years of Tory cuts.
UK gambling firms' value jumps after chancellor resisted large duty hike
Rob Davies
Machine games duty (MGD) is the tax levied on slot machines found in bookmakers, casinos, bingo halls and adult gaming centres (AGCs). The chancellor faced calls to double the rate of MGD from 20% to 40%, a policy backed by one of his predecessors, Gordon Brown.
Amid fierce lobbying from gambling firms, which issued dire warnings of thousands of job cuts, Healey opted for a more modest rise to 25% today. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.
Investors responded with relief, adding £240m to the combined stock market value of Entain (Ladbrokes/Coral), Evoke (William Hill), RankGroup (Mecca Bingo/Grosvenor Casinos) and Playtech (designer of slot machine games). Entain said the MGC hike will cost it £25m, which it expects to be able to mitigate, including by shop closures. Betfred boss Fred Done, whose family took a £30m dividend from their betting empire earlier this year, also warned that closures and job losses would follow.
The chancellor singled out AGCs, sometimes known as “slot farms” for particular attention. As well as the duty rise, they will also be excluded - along with vape shops - from business rates relief available to retail and hospitality businesses.
Burnham rules out general election in the next year
Andy Burnham has ruled out calling a snap general election in the next year amid ongoing speculation (including among economists and investors) that he could seek to consolidate his position.
He said he was thinking “about people” and not “my own party and its prospects”, Press Association reports.
The prime minister was asked if he would call an election in the next year as he visited a community centre in central London after the Budget.
He said:
“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months.
“I have said repeatedly since coming into this job, I’m not thinking about myself. I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects.
“I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them to have that care for people, which I spoke about on my first day in Downing Street.”
He added that he was “leading from the front” and “putting Britain on a different path”.
He said:
“We’ve got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage.”
Several City economists are suggesting that today’s budget may be teeing up an early general election.
AndrewWishart, senior UK economist at Berenberg, suggests there is a 40% chance of a general election before the end of 2027.
He points out that this would allow Labour to discard its previous manifesto commitments not to raise taxes on working people.
Wishart says:
The big questions, about how to fund a national social care service and a £15bn increase in defence spending by 2030 remain unanswered. The government will hope that the combination of a decline in gilt yields a reduction in transfer payments to those with disabilities and efficiency savings enable them to fund their priorities without a major increase in taxes. It’s just about possible, but pretty unlikely and requires tax hikes pencilled in for the back end of the parliament to come in, potentially just before the next general election.
More ambition would require a new mandate without the manifesto constraint on tax, achieved by via a general election. We put the chances of one before the end of next year at about 40%.”
Eoin O’Callaghan, macro strategist at Wellington Management, says there is a “significant question mark” over the credibility of the projections, including the biig squeeze on departmental spending in a few year’s time.
Like last autumn’s budget they incorporate an unrealistic real term freeze in departmental spending in 2029-30, after the next election. And they now incorporate an even more challenging 3% real terms cut to next year’s departmental spending too to help offset rising interest rate and unfunded public sector pensions costs. The forecasts are also predicated on nominal growth staying relatively elevated close to 4% throughout the forecast.
“That may not concern the market for now. But it highlights how challenging the UK public finances are. How difficult the fiscal decisions ahead of this government are. And why there is a risk of early elections given the tough spending decisions ahead.”
BenjaminJones, Invesco’s Global Head of Research, predicts speculation about an early election will continue to build:
“After two blockbuster, tax-hiking budgets, investors will welcome this more ‘steady as she goes’ package from the new Labour Chancellor. Against a backdrop of rising gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty, Healey’s decision to limit spending increases and tax rises shows sensible caution.
His opening comments were clearly aimed to ease bond market fears. However, many of the difficult fiscal choices - such as delivering welfare savings and boosting Defence spending - have been postponed until the Spending Review next year, which will continue to fuel speculation of an early election.
John Healey announced a first-time buyer ISA in his speech. This is what the Treasury says about how it will work.
The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

title: US: Department of Homeland Security data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
content_c:
US: DHS data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
October 29, 2026
In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website.
Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew."
DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available.
Transparency group says releasing data justified
The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from:
- Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
- Customs and Border Protection (CBP)
- US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
- Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)
- the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
- other DHS agencies
The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data.
Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website.
Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight.
According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details.
DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.
The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months.
Third serious data breach recently
This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks:
- Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel
- In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees.

title: Brasiliens Wahlverlierer: Bolsonaros spektakuläre Flucht
content_c:
Brasiliens Wahlverlierer Bolsonaros spektakuläre Flucht
Ein Privatflugzeug, Zwischenstopps, die Ankunft in den USA - der brasilianische Wahlverlierer Bolsonaro ist nun in Florida - und bezeichnet sich als "Anführer" Brasiliens. Wie geht das rechte Lager mit dem geflüchteten Bolsonaro um?
Es ist 9:24 Uhr am Mittwochmorgen, als auf dem Privatflughafen von Opa-Locka nördlich von Miami eine Privatmaschine landet. Es steigen aus: Flávio Bolsonaro, seine Frau und die beiden Töchter. Damit endet das Rätselraten über den Verbleib des 45-Jährigen.
Noch am Montag hatte er wenige Stunden nach seiner Wahlniederlage erklärt, er werde Brasilien nicht verlassen. "Ich werde die Opposition organisieren. Wir haben die Mehrheit im Senat und in der Abgeordnetenkammer erreicht. Lasst uns den Kopf heben und weiter für unser Brasilien kämpfen", sagte Bolsonaro.
"Was auch immer geschieht: Wir werden unser Brasilien nicht aufgeben."
Spektakuläre Flucht
Doch am Dienstag überschlagen sich die Meldungen: argentinische Medien spekulieren über eine Ausreise über Puerto Iguazú nahe den gleichnamigen Wasserfällen an der brasilianischen Grenze.
Am Abend heißt es, Bolsonaro sei bereits in den USA - anonyme Quellen munkelten, Behörden dementierten.
All das sollte wohl vertuschen, dass die Flucht noch in Planung war. Denn der Oberste Gericht hatte ein Ausreiseverbot gegen Bolsonaro verhängt, mit der Anordnung, seine Pässe abzugeben.
Stattdessen nutze der 45-jährige Senator wohl seinen italienischen Pass, um Dienstagnacht nach Argentinien und von dort weiter in die USA zu reisen, wohl mit Zwischenstopp Ecuador.
Die USA erklärten sich zur Aufnahme Bolsonaros bereit und haben ihm und seiner Familie Visa ausgestellt. Dazu erklärte Trump noch vor Bolsonaros Landung. "Ich halte sie für anständige Leute. Die Wahl war sehr seltsam, und ich fand sie schrecklich. Sie hat schlechte Kritiken bekommen."
Geldwäsche, Korruption, Steuerhinterziehung
Wie anständig Flávio Bolsonaro tatsächlich ist, dazu ermittelt allerdings Brasiliens Justiz. Es geht um Geldwäsche, Korruption und Steuerhinterziehung. Einmal untersuchen die Behörden Bolsonaros Beziehung zum inzwischen inhaftierten Banker Daniel Vorcaro. Der steht im Zentrum des größten Betrugsskandals der jüngeren Geschichte Brasiliens. Von ihm soll Flávio Geld für die Finanzierung eines Films über seinen Vater - den wegen eines Putschversuchs inhaftierten Ex-Präsidenten Jair Bolsonaro -, erbeten und davon 20 Millionen abgezwackt haben.
Dazu soll er mit einem befreundeten Anwalt auch in Geldwäsche rund um Sportwetten verwickelt sein. Es geht um umgerechnet 1,1 Milliarden Euro. Bolsonaro bestreitet die Vorwürfe - seine Anhänger verbreiten im Netz die Narrative des politisch Verfolgten durch eine vom linken Lula beeinflusste Justiz.
Der politische Analyst ordnet dies im TV-Kanal Globo anders ein. Octavio Guedes sagt dort: "Flávio Bolsonaro flieht aus einem Land, in dem er frei kandidieren konnte. Ja, er flieht aus einem Land, in dem sein Bruder Senator ist. Er flieht aus einem Land, in dem ein weiterer Bruder Abgeordneter im Bundesparlament ist. Er verlässt ein Land, in dem seine Partei die Mehrheit im Abgeordnetenhaus stellt. Er flieht also vor einer Demokratie. Er flieht vor der Auseinandersetzung mit der Justiz - um nichts anderes geht es."
Präsident - oder Anführer - oder gar nichts?
Im Februar endet Bolsonaros Mandat als Senator, dann verliert er die parlamentarische Immunität. Als gewählter Präsident wären Ermittlungen gegen ihn nur mit Zustimmung des Kongresses möglich gewesen, in dem Bolsonaros liberale Partei PL stärkste Kraft ist.
Den Wahlsieg Lula da Silvas hat Bolsonaro selbst bis heute nicht öffentlich anerkannt - seine Partei dagegen schon. Am Mittwochabend postete er dann, bereits aus den USA, ein Kommuniqué auf X. Darin bezeichnet er sich als den "wahren gewählten Präsidenten" und spricht von Wahlbetrug bei der Stichwahl am 25. Oktober. Dabei verglich er sich mit Venezuelas Interimspräsident Juan Guaidó und Charles de Gaulle, dem französischen Präsidenten der Nachkriegsjahre. Kurze Zeit später korrigierte er die Formulierung zu "Anführer".
"Zeit, dass sich das rechte Lager äußert"
Das Bild des gemäßigten Bolsonaro, als der sich Flávio im Wahlkampf präsentiert habe, sei damit als Fassade entlarvt, sagt Joao Paulo Charleaux, Experte für internationale Beziehungen. "Eine Wahl, die - laut Flávio Bolsonaro und sonst niemandem - gestohlen wurde. Wollen all die Parlamentarier und Gouverneure der Rechten tatsächlich auf ihre errungenen Mandate verzichten, weil sie glauben, die Wahl sei gestohlen worden? Die Antwort lautet: nein. Der Einzige, der unzufrieden ist, ist Flávio - er hat nämlich verloren."
Es sei an der Zeit, dass sich Brasiliens rechtes Lager dazu äußere. Wer sich bereits äußerte, ist US-Präsident Donald Trump. Auf das Schreiben Bolsonaros angesprochen, erklärte er, er werde dieses nicht kommentieren. Er habe Bolsonaro die Genehmigung erteilt, ins Land zu kommen, werde sich aber weiter nicht einmischen.
Und in Brasilien erklärte Tarcísio de Freitas, wiedergewählter Gouverneur von São Paulo und einflussreicher Politiker des rechten Lagers, gegenüber der Zeitung Estadao, er verstehe "die Gefühle, die Empörung und den Zorn" Bolsonaros, aber der richtige Weg sei, das Wahlergebnis zu respektieren und nach vorne zu blicken.

content_c:
Netanjahu bei Wahl in Israel vorn - ohne Regierungsmehrheit
Veröffentlicht 28. Oktober 2026Zuletzt aktualisiert 28. Oktober 2026
Mit der höchsten Wahlbeteiligung seit 1999 hat Israel ein neues Parlament gewählt. Fast 78 Prozent der rund 7,3 Millionen Wahlberechtigten gaben am Dienstag ihre Stimme ab. Doch nach Auszählung von mehr als 80 Prozent der Stimmen gibt es noch keinen klaren Sieger.
Das Lager von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu führt derzeit mit 53 Sitzen vor dem Oppositionsblock unter Gadi Eisenkot, der auf 48 Mandate kommt; die Listen der arabischen Parteien erreichen 19 Sitze. Diese Teilergebnisse können sich allerdings noch ändern.
"Rechtsgerichtete, nationale, starke Regierung"
In der Nacht zu Mittwoch sagte Netanjahu in Jerusalem, der Block mit seiner Likud-Partei verfüge über eine klare und entscheidende Mehrheit "in der jüdischen Bevölkerung und bei all jenen, die den Staat unterstützen". Er forderte eine "rechtsgerichtete, nationale, starke Regierung" und warnte vor einem möglichen Bündnis der Gegner mit den arabischen Parteien, denen er eine israelfeindliche Haltung vorwarf.
Mit Blick auf den verfeindeten Iran erklärte Netanjahu, er sei fest entschlossen, gemeinsam mit US-Präsident Donald Trump die iranische Bedrohung ein für alle Mal zu beenden. Bei der vorigen Wahl 2022 hatte seine Koalition, die sich zuletzt auf rechtsextreme und streng religiöse Parteien stützte, noch 64 Sitze errungen.
Der 77-Jährige ist mit Unterbrechungen seit 19 Jahren im Amt. Erstmals war er von 1996 bis 1999 Ministerpräsident. Später folgte eine weitere Amtszeit von 2009 bis 2021, ehe Netanjahu 2022 erneut Regierungschef wurde.
"Sicherheit des Landes nicht für politische Zwecke missbrauchen"
Eisenkot warnte Netanjahu davor, die Sicherheit des Landes für politische Zwecke zu missbrauchen. Der ehemalige Generalstabschef sagte, Netanjahu sei nur noch ein geschäftsführender Ministerpräsident ohne Mandat oder das Vertrauen des Volkes. Der Sicherheitsapparat müsse allen Versuchen widerstehen, politische Interessen über die Sicherheit Israels zu stellen.
Mehrere Nachwahlbefragungen hatten bereits ein Kopf-an-Kopf-Rennen zwischen beiden Lagern prognostiziert, bei denen keiner der Blöcke die nötige absolute Mehrheit erreicht. Diese liegt bei 61 der 120 Sitze in der Knesset. Die Abstimmung gilt als richtungsweisend in dem stark gespaltenen Land. Wichtigste Themen im Wahlkampf waren die Aufarbeitung des Großangriffs der islamistischen Hamas vom 7. Oktober 2023, radikale Siedler im besetzten Westjordanland und der Wehrdienst für ultraorthodoxe Juden.
Die Hamas hatte am 7. Oktober 2023 ein Massaker auf israelischem Gebiet verübt, dem nach Angaben des Militärs etwa 1200 Menschen zum Opfer fielen. Rund 250 Personen wurden als Geiseln in den Gazastreifen verschleppt. Beim darauffolgenden israelischen Militäreinsatz wurden nach Zahlen der Hamas-Behörden mehr als 74.000 Menschen in dem Palästinensergebiet getötet. Dabei wird nicht zwischen Kämpfern und Zivilisten unterschieden. Die Hamas wird von zahlreichen Staaten als Terrororganisation eingestuft.
Auftrag zur Regierungsbildung innerhalb von 14 Tagen
Spätestens in einer Woche muss das amtliche Endergebnis der Wahl veröffentlicht werden. Danach wird Präsident Izchak Herzog binnen sieben Tagen einen Abgeordneten mit der Regierungsbildung beauftragen. In der Regel ist es der Politiker, dem die besten Chancen eingeräumt werden - voraussichtlich Likud-Chef Netanjahu oder der Vorsitzende der Jaschar-Partei, Eisenkot.
Der erste Versuch einer Regierungsbildung müsste bis Ende November abgeschlossen sein. Präsident Herzog entscheidet, ob es noch einmal eine Verlängerung von 14 Tagen gibt. Diese Frist würde dann spätestens Mitte Dezember ablaufen.
Scheitert der erste Anlauf, bekommt der zweite Kandidat den Auftrag. Eine Verlängerung wäre dann nach 28 Tagen nicht mehr möglich. Im Anschluss könnten noch mindestens 61 Abgeordnete des neu gewählten Parlaments, das sich bis zum 10. November konstituiert, innerhalb von drei Wochen einen Kandidaten vorschlagen. Dieser müsste innerhalb von 14 Tagen eine Regierung bilden.
Führen alle drei Etappen nicht zu einer mehrheitsfähigen Regierungskoalition, löst sich das Parlament automatisch auf. In diesem Fall schließen sich Neuwahlen innerhalb einer Frist von 90 Tagen an. Diese würden somit bis spätestens Mitte April 2027 abgehalten. Der amtierende Ministerpräsident Netanjahu bliebe bis dahin an der Spitze einer Übergangsregierung.
Anschlag auf israelische Botschaft in der Wahlnacht
Unterdessen wurde vor der israelischen Botschaft in Belgrad ein Minderjähriger erschossen, nachdem er mutmaßlich einen Polizisten angegriffen hatte. Der serbische Innenminister Ivica Dacic sprach von einem "terroristischen Angriff" in der Nacht zum Mittwoch.
Der mutmaßliche Täter habe den Beamten mit zwei Messern attackiert und dabei "Allahu Akbar" ("Gott ist der Größte") gerufen, erklärte Dacic. Der Polizist habe Stichverletzungen im Gesicht davongetragen. Er habe den Angreifer in Notwehr getötet.
Dacic zufolge wurde der Angreifer von den Sicherheitsbehörden überwacht. Er habe in sozialen Medien eine schwarze Flagge und das Emblem der Terrororganisation "Islamischer Staat" veröffentlicht.
Das israelische Außenministerium bestätigte einen "versuchten Terroranschlag" nahe der Botschaft in Serbien. Die diplomatische Vertretung sei zum Zeitpunkt des Vorfalls geschlossen gewesen.
jj/pg/haz (dpa, afp, rtr, kna)

title: Олександр Рудинський після знімань закордоном розкрив, якими насправді є голлівудські зірки
content_c:
Олександр Рудинський після знімань закордоном розкрив, якими насправді є голлівудські зірки
Актор пригадав незвичайний досвід на міжнародному знімальному майданчику та розповів, що його вразило у роботі з оскароносними колегами.
Український актор Олександр Рудинський поділився подробицями роботи з голлівудськими зірками Едрієном Броуді та Шоном Пенном.
Артист зіграв у міжнародному проєкті «Зміїний острів» режисера Дага Лаймана, присвяченому подіям навколо підриву газопроводів «Північний потік — 2». Знімальний процес відбувався в Болгарії та Хорватії, зокрема у відкритому морі. В інтерв’ю для шоу «Наодинці з Гламуром» Рудинський уперше розповів, якими запам’ятав своїх знаменитих колег і що найбільше вразило його на майданчику.
Актор зізнався, що давно захоплюється творчістю Броуді, тому можливість попрацювати з ним стала особливим досвідом. За словами Рудинського, голлівудський артист виявився приємною людиною, а під час підготовки до стрічки команда серйозно досліджувала український контекст. Режисер Даг Лайман самостійно працював над сценарієм і міг змінювати сцени безпосередньо під час знімального процесу. Через це акторам доводилося бути готовими до несподіваних рішень. Окремим випробуванням для Рудинського стали зйомки у відкритому морі, де він уперше зіткнувся з морською хворобою.
«Це один з моїх найулюбленіших акторів», — поділився Олександр про Броуді.
Особливо яскраво Рудинський пригадав момент, коли опинився неподалік від сцени за участю Броуді та Пеннa. Поки актор чекав на власний епізод, його колеги працювали над спільною сценою. Українець слухав їхню гру в навушниках і спостерігав за робочим процесом.
«У людей п’ять „Оскарів“ на двох. А я сидів отак от наушниках, просто слухав, як вони грають. Іноді плутаються в тексті. Щоб ви просто розуміли, що це живі люди», — розповів артист.
Рудинський також згадав, що мав нагоду поспілкуватися з Пенном. Він є прихильником його роботи у фільмі «Одна битва за іншою» й хотів обговорити стрічку з актором. Під час зустрічі американець подарував йому пачку цигарок, а Броуді також долучився до збору, про який розповів українець.
Водночас Рудинський зізнався, що поки не впевнений, чи міжнародний фільм зрештою вийде на екрани. Він сподівається на прем’єру у 2027 році, однак побоюється, що через політичний контекст проєкт можуть відкласти. Актор наголосив, що підтримує позицію своєї країни в питанні підриву газопроводів, адже українці та німці по-різному оцінюють ці події.
Про це Олександр Рудинський розповів журналістці Анні Севастьяновій у новому випуску шоу «Наодинці з Гламуром».
▶️ Повний випуск «Наодинці з Гламуром» можна подивитися за цим посиланням: 
"Теж плутаються у тексті": РУДИНСЬКИЙ вперше про роботу з БРОУДІ і ПЕННОМ. Прем’єра кіно ЗА ПЕРЕМОГУ
Нагадаємо, нещодавно Костянтин Темляк вперше з’явився на публіці після скандальних звинувачень у насильстві.

title: Ушаков о трехсторонних переговорах: «Дата встречи будет зависеть от ситуации на поле боя»
content_c:
Помощник главы Кремля Юрий Ушаков заявил, что трехсторонние консультации между Россией, США и Украиной состоятся не раньше чем после 4 ноября. Кроме того, по его словам, вопрос определения даты встречи «будет зависеть от ситуации на поле боя и общей обстановки», пишут российские СМИ.
В частности, комментируя заявление премьер-министра Польши Дональда Туска о возможном проведении трехсторонних консультаций 4 ноября, Ушаков отметил, что российская сторона пока не передавала никаких сигналов по этому поводу. Также он сообщил, что состав российской делегации объявят позже.
«У нас есть костяк, конечно, но состав, думаю, определят в ближайшее время», — сказал он.
Ушаков уточнил, что переговоры планируется провести с участием представителей России, Украины и США, подчеркнув, что «речь идет именно о представителях этих стран».
После встречи российского диктатора Владимира Путина со специальным посланником американского президента Стивом Уиткоффом 21 октября стало известно, что Россия готова вернуться к трехсторонним переговорам с участием США и Украины. Ушаков также отметил, что следующий раунд встреч может пройти в Абу-Даби.
Президент Владимир Зеленский заявлял, что Киев хочет, чтобы трехсторонняя встреча Украины, США и России в Абу-Даби состоялась до возможной встречи США, Китая и России. title: Як військові Росії перейшли лінію фронту та їхали автостопом до Києва
content_c:
Як військові Росії перейшли лінію фронту та їхали автостопом до Києва
Контррозвідка СБУ затримала на Донеччині двох контрактників 291-го мотострілецького полку Південного військового округу Росії, які втекли з фронту та під виглядом цивільних намагалися дістатися до Києва.
Це вже другий випадок за останні місяці, коли військові РФ переходять лінію фронту та прямують до українських міст. На початку жовтня така спроба росіянина звершилась трагедією - він вбив шістьох людей перед тим, як його затримали у Харкові.
Зараз, за даними слідства, російських військових зупинили на блокпості під час в'їзду до Дніпропетровської області. Вони їхали в автомобілі, який зупинили автостопом. У одного із затриманих на шиї виявили жетон військовослужбовця армії Росії.
Як встановили правоохоронці, обидва нещодавно могли брати участь у штурмі позицій українських військових на Краматорському напрямку. Згодом вони залишили лінію бойового зіткнення, дісталися одного із населених пунктів у "сірій зоні", переодягнулися в цивільний одяг, а військову форму, зброю та спорядження закопали.
Після цього чоловіки пішки вирушили до райцентру, де зупинили автомобіль. СБУ каже, що водій погодився підвезти їх до Дніпра, звідки вони планували дістатися столиці. За інформацією СБУ, один із втікачів мав у Києві родичів і розраховував там переховуватися.
Серед затриманих виявився мешканець тимчасово окупованого Довжанська Луганської області, який двічі був засуджений за вбивство та воює на боці Росії з 2016 року. Після початку повномасштабного вторгнення він брав участь у боях під Бахмутом як помічник навідника протитанкового ракетного комплексу.
Другий фігурант - громадянин Росії. За даними слідства, він підписав контракт із російським міноборони під час відбування покарання за вбивство.
Жителю Луганщини повідомили про підозру за статтями про державну зраду та колабораційну діяльність. Суд обрав йому запобіжний захід у вигляді тримання під вартою без права внесення застави. Йому загрожує довічне ув'язнення з конфіскацією майна.
Громадянина Росії наразі утримують як військовополоненого. Розслідування триває.
Вбивство бійців ЗСУ на Харківщині
Це не вперше, коли російські військові потрапляють в українські тилові міста.
13 жовтня у Харківській області російський військовослужбовець, за даними слідства, застрелив п'ятьох військових ЗСУ та одного цивільного чоловіка.
Спочатку правоохоронці повідомляли, що нападник міг бути військовополоненим, який утік із місця утримання, однак згодом СБУ заявила, що він самовільно залишив позиції російських військ на фронті та кілька днів переховувався на території області.
За версією слідства, спочатку чоловік застрелив 60-річного місцевого жителя біля водойми, а потім проник до будинку в селі Момотове, де перебували п'ятеро українських військовослужбовців, і відкрив по них вогонь.
Наступного дня підозрюваного затримали в Харкові. Ним виявився 36-річний військовий армії РФ Леонід Рижиков. Йому оголосили підозру у вчиненні воєнного злочину, що спричинив загибель людей.

title: Поріг боргу за комуналку, через який можуть забрати єдине житло, зріс до понад 430 тис. грн – Мін'юст
content_c:
З 23 жовтня в Україні діє підвищений поріг боргу за комунальні послуги, за який можуть забрати єдине житло: замість 170 тис. грн він становить понад 430 тис. грн, повідомляє Міністерство юстиції.
"Отже, щоб у тебе забрали єдине житло, потрібно дуже постаратися накопичити борги за комуналку. Таких комунальних боржників буквально одиниці. Тобто за комунальні борги у 99,999% випадків єдине житло забирати не будуть. Тут я хочу заспокоїти людей", – цитує відомство заступника міністра юстиції з питань виконавчої служби Андрія Гайченка.
Відповідні положення передбачені законом №4833-IX. За розрахунками Мін'юсту, за щомісячної плати за комунальні послуги 6 тис. грн для накопичення такого боргу знадобиться шість років несплати. Водночас навіть перевищення цієї суми не означає автоматичного стягнення житла.
Закон також гарантує додатковий захист єдиного житла військовослужбовців, а для боржників за житлово-комунальні послуги на територіях активних бойових дій і тимчасово окупованих територіях – окремі гарантії під час виконавчого провадження.
Джерело: https://t.me/minjustofficial/7120

title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
content_c:
Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
- Published
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.
With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.
Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.
- How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority 
  - Published19 hours ago
During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.
"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.
He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.
Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.
"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."
Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.
Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".
"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."
As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.
Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.
Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.
Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results.
"I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."
She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.
Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".
He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".
Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.
The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Mahdi Kabaha who lives in a village near Haifa and campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic".
"Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.
The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".
Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.
United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".
The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it.

content:
Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
- Published
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.
With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.
Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.
- How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority 
  - Published19 hours ago
During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.
"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.
He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.
Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.
"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."
Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.
Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".
"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."
As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.
Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.
Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.
Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results.
"I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."
She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.
Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".
He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".
Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.
The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Mahdi Kabaha who lives in a village near Haifa and campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic".
"Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.
The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".
Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.
United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".
The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it.
"The opposition parties cannot dictate any conditions," Jabareen said. "If the opposition in Israel are willing to afford real and substantive change, and an alternative for the dangerous, extreme-right-wing government... they will have to negotiate with us."
